blocks.body:
Rabbits and foxes share an island. More rabbits feed more foxes; more foxes eat more rabbits. Write $x$ and $y$ for the two populations and you get a pair of differential equations that no one can solve with a formula. Yet a simple picture shows that the populations cycle forever around a fixed centre.

This page is about those pictures. Instead of graphing $x$ and $y$ against time, we plot the point $(x(t), y(t))$ as it moves in the plane. The linear theory from [[ode-systems]] describes the motion near each equilibrium, [[partial-derivatives]] give the linearisation, and Lyapunov's method handles what linearisation cannot.

blocks.title: Autonomous systems and their trajectories
blocks.body:
A two-dimensional autonomous system is

$$x' = f(x, y), \qquad y' = g(x, y),$$

where $f$ and $g$ do not depend on $t$. At each point the right side is a vector, the velocity of a solution passing through that point. A solution traces a curve, its trajectory or orbit, which is everywhere tangent to this vector field. The phase portrait is the collection of trajectories.

If $f$ and $g$ have continuous partial derivatives, solutions of initial value problems are unique, and since the system is autonomous, a time-shifted solution is again a solution. It follows that two different trajectories never cross: if they shared a point, the solutions through it would agree up to a time shift. So there are only three kinds of trajectory: equilibrium points, closed curves (periodic solutions), and curves that never repeat.

Two tools help to sketch. An equilibrium (critical point) is a point where $f = g = 0$; the constant function sitting there is a solution. The nullclines are the curves $f = 0$, where trajectories move vertically, and $g = 0$, where they move horizontally. They cut the plane into regions in which the signs of $x'$ and $y'$, and so the rough direction of motion, are fixed; equilibria lie where nullclines of different kinds meet.

blocks.title: The linear picture
blocks.body:
For $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ with $A$ a real $2\times2$ matrix and $\det A \ne 0$, the origin is the only equilibrium. Write $\tau = \operatorname{tr}A$ and $\Delta = \det A$. The eigenvalues are the roots of $\lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \Delta = 0$, so $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = \Delta$ and $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = \tau$, and the solutions are combinations of $e^{\lambda t}$ times vectors.

- Saddle ($\Delta < 0$): real eigenvalues of opposite sign. Solutions approach along the eigenvector of the negative eigenvalue and leave along the other; all others pass by, like hyperbolas.
- Node ($\Delta > 0$, $\tau^2 \ge 4\Delta$): real eigenvalues of the same sign. All trajectories enter (if $\tau < 0$) or leave (if $\tau > 0$) the origin; apart from the two along the other eigenvector, they do so tangent to the eigenvector of the eigenvalue smaller in absolute value, the slow direction. When $\tau^2 = 4\Delta$ the eigenvalue is repeated and the node is degenerate or a star.
- Spiral ($\Delta > 0$, $0 < \tau^2 < 4\Delta$): complex eigenvalues $\alpha \pm i\beta$ with $\alpha = \tau/2 \ne 0$. Trajectories wind around the origin, inward if $\tau < 0$, outward if $\tau > 0$.
- Centre ($\Delta > 0$, $\tau = 0$): purely imaginary eigenvalues. All trajectories are closed ellipses around the origin.

So the origin attracts every solution exactly when $\tau < 0$ and $\Delta > 0$. The parabola $\tau^2 = 4\Delta$ and the lines $\Delta = 0$ and $\tau = 0$ divide the trace–determinant plane into the regions above; the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ from [[ode-systems]] has $\tau = 2$, $\Delta = -3$ and is a saddle.

blocks.title: Stability
blocks.body:
An equilibrium $\mathbf x^*$ is stable (in the sense of Lyapunov) if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that every solution with $|\mathbf x(0) - \mathbf x^*| < \delta$ satisfies $|\mathbf x(t) - \mathbf x^*| < \varepsilon$ for all $t \ge 0$. It is asymptotically stable if it is stable and moreover $\mathbf x(t) \to \mathbf x^*$ for all solutions starting close enough. It is unstable if it is not stable.

Stable means 'start close, stay close'; asymptotically stable adds 'and come back'. A centre is stable but not asymptotically stable.

blocks.title: Linearisation
blocks.body:
Let $\mathbf x^*$ be an equilibrium of $\mathbf x' = \mathbf F(\mathbf x)$, with $\mathbf F$ continuously differentiable, and let $J = D\mathbf F(\mathbf x^*)$ be the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives there.

1. If every eigenvalue of $J$ has negative real part, $\mathbf x^*$ is asymptotically stable. If some eigenvalue has positive real part, $\mathbf x^*$ is unstable.
2. (Hartman–Grobman) If no eigenvalue of $J$ has zero real part, then near $\mathbf x^*$ there is a continuous change of coordinates carrying the trajectories of the nonlinear system onto those of $\mathbf y' = J\mathbf y$, preserving the direction of time. In particular a saddle stays a saddle, with exactly two trajectories entering and two leaving. (A homeomorphism cannot tell a node from a spiral, so this part is silent on that distinction. A direct estimate of the angle swept by nearby trajectories shows that a spiral of $J$ stays a spiral and a node of $J$ with two distinct eigenvalues stays a node; only when $J$ has a repeated real eigenvalue can the nonlinear terms turn a node into a spiral.)

If $J$ has an eigenvalue with zero real part (a linear centre, or a zero eigenvalue), the linearisation decides nothing: the nonlinear terms do.

blocks.title: Why linearisation works
blocks.body: Write $\mathbf x = \mathbf x^* + \mathbf u$. By Taylor's theorem $\mathbf F(\mathbf x^* + \mathbf u) = J\mathbf u + \mathbf r(\mathbf u)$ with $|\mathbf r(\mathbf u)|/|\mathbf u| \to 0$, so near the equilibrium the remainder is tiny compared with the linear term. As a heuristic, think of the nonlinear terms as a small perturbation of $J$. Saddles, spirals and nodes with distinct eigenvalues fill open regions of the $\tau$–$\Delta$ plane, so a small perturbation cannot change their type. The borderline cases can tip: a centre ($\tau = 0$) may become a stable or unstable spiral or stay a centre, and a node with a repeated eigenvalue (on the parabola $\tau^2 = 4\Delta$) may become a spiral. (Part 1 in the stable case is proved with a quadratic Lyapunov function $\mathbf u^TP\mathbf u$ for the linear system; see the next theorem.)

blocks.title: Lyapunov's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\mathbf x^*$ be an equilibrium of $\mathbf x' = \mathbf F(\mathbf x)$ and let $V$ be continuously differentiable on a neighbourhood $U$ of $\mathbf x^*$, with $V(\mathbf x^*) = 0$ and $V(\mathbf x) > 0$ for $\mathbf x \ne \mathbf x^*$ in $U$. Let $\dot V = \nabla V\cdot\mathbf F$ be the rate of change of $V$ along solutions.

1. If $\dot V \le 0$ on $U$, then $\mathbf x^*$ is stable.
2. If $\dot V < 0$ on $U \setminus \{\mathbf x^*\}$, then $\mathbf x^*$ is asymptotically stable.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Take $\mathbf x^* = 0$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small enough that the closed ball $\bar B_\varepsilon$ lies in $U$. On the circle $|\mathbf x| = \varepsilon$, which is compact, $V$ has a positive minimum $m$. By continuity of $V$ at $0$ there is $\delta < \varepsilon$ with $V < m$ on $B_\delta$. Along a solution starting in $B_\delta$, $\frac{d}{dt}V(\mathbf x(t)) = \dot V \le 0$, so $V(\mathbf x(t)) \le V(\mathbf x(0)) < m$ for as long as the solution stays in $U$. It can therefore never reach the circle $|\mathbf x| = \varepsilon$, where $V \ge m$, so it stays in $B_\varepsilon$ for all $t \ge 0$. This proves 1.

For 2, $V(\mathbf x(t))$ is decreasing and bounded below, so it tends to a limit $c \ge 0$. Suppose $c > 0$. Then the solution stays in the set $K = \{\mathbf x : |\mathbf x| \le \varepsilon,\ V(\mathbf x) \ge c\}$, which is compact and does not contain $0$. On $K$ the continuous function $\dot V$ is negative, so it is at most some $-k < 0$, and then $V(\mathbf x(t)) \le V(\mathbf x(0)) - kt$, which becomes negative: a contradiction. So $V(\mathbf x(t)) \to 0$. Finally, if $\mathbf x(t)$ did not tend to $0$, there would be times $t_n \to \infty$ with $\eta \le |\mathbf x(t_n)| \le \varepsilon$ for some $\eta > 0$, and there $V \ge \min_{\eta \le |\mathbf x| \le \varepsilon}V > 0$, contradicting $V(\mathbf x(t_n)) \to 0$.

blocks.title: Conservative systems
blocks.body:
Sometimes there is a function $H(x,y)$ that is constant along every solution, a conserved quantity or first integral: $\dot H = H_xf + H_yg = 0$. Then trajectories lie on level curves of $H$: the phase portrait is a contour map. Near a strict local minimum or maximum of $H$ the level curves are small closed loops, so an equilibrium there is a nonlinear centre, surrounded by periodic orbits.

The undamped pendulum $\theta'' = -\sin\theta$, written as $x = \theta$, $y = \theta'$, is $x' = y$, $y' = -\sin x$. The energy $H = \frac12y^2 - \cos x$ is conserved. Equilibria are $(k\pi, 0)$. At $(0, 0)$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, a linear centre, and $H$ has a strict minimum there, so small swings are periodic. At $(\pi, 0)$ the Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, with $\Delta = -1$: a saddle, the pendulum balanced upside down. The level curve $H = 1$ through the saddles, the separatrix, divides back-and-forth swinging ($H < 1$) from swinging over the top ($H > 1$). With friction, $y' = -\sin x - cy$ with $c > 0$, we get $\dot H = -cy^2 \le 0$: the energy is a Lyapunov function, and the centres become stable spirals (for small $c$).

blocks.title: Competing species
blocks.body: Two species compete for food: $x' = x(3 - x - 2y)$, $y' = y(2 - x - y)$ with $x, y \ge 0$. Find and classify the equilibria and describe the long-term outcome.
blocks.solution:
Equilibria: $x = 0$ or $x + 2y = 3$, together with $y = 0$ or $x + y = 2$. This gives $(0,0)$, $(0, 2)$, $(3, 0)$ and, solving $x + 2y = 3$, $x + y = 2$, the coexistence point $(1, 1)$.

The Jacobian is $J = \begin{pmatrix}3 - 2x - 2y & -2x\\ -y & 2 - x - 2y\end{pmatrix}$.

- At $(0,0)$: $\operatorname{diag}(3, 2)$, an unstable node.
- At $(3,0)$: $\begin{pmatrix}-3 & -6\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $-3, -1$: a stable node.
- At $(0,2)$: $\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 0\\ -2 & -2\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $-1, -2$: a stable node.
- At $(1,1)$: $\begin{pmatrix}-1 & -2\\ -1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, $\Delta = -1 < 0$: a saddle, with eigenvalues $-1 \pm \sqrt2$.

All of these are hyperbolic, so linearisation is reliable. The two trajectories that enter the saddle (its stable manifold) form a curve through $(1,1)$ separating the quadrant into two basins: from one side, solutions go to $(3, 0)$ and species $y$ dies out; from the other, they go to $(0, 2)$. Coexistence is possible only on the separating curve itself, which is unstable. This is competitive exclusion: when competition between the species is strong compared with competition within each, one species wins, and which one depends on the starting populations.

blocks.title: Predators and prey
blocks.body: For $x' = x(3 - y)$, $y' = y(x - 2)$ with $x, y > 0$ (prey $x$, predators $y$), show that every trajectory other than the equilibrium is a closed curve.
blocks.solution:
The only equilibrium with $x, y > 0$ is $(2, 3)$. Its Jacobian is $\begin{pmatrix}3 - y & -x\\ y & x - 2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -2\\ 3 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, with $\tau = 0$ and $\Delta = 6$: a linear centre, which by itself proves nothing.

Divide the equations: $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y(x-2)}{x(3-y)}$, which separates as $\frac{3 - y}{y}\,dy = \frac{x - 2}{x}\,dx$. So

$$H(x,y) = x - 2\ln x + y - 3\ln y$$

should be conserved; indeed $\dot H = \bigl(1 - \frac2x\bigr)x(3 - y) + \bigl(1 - \frac3y\bigr)y(x - 2) = (x - 2)(3 - y) + (y - 3)(x - 2) = 0$.

Now $H$ is a sum of a function of $x$ alone, which is strictly convex with minimum at $x = 2$, and a function of $y$ alone, strictly convex with minimum at $y = 3$; both tend to $+\infty$ at $0$ and at $\infty$. So each level set $H = c$ above the minimum value is a single closed curve around $(2, 3)$. A trajectory lies on such a curve and cannot stop (there is no equilibrium on it), so it goes round and round: the populations oscillate periodically. Small oscillations have angular frequency $\sqrt\Delta = \sqrt6$.

blocks.title: When linearisation is silent
blocks.body: (a) Show that the origin is asymptotically stable for $x' = -y - x^3$, $y' = x - y^3$, but unstable for $x' = -y + x^3$, $y' = x + y^3$, although both have the same linearisation. (b) For the hard spring $x' = y$, $y' = -x^3$, show that all solutions are periodic, and find how the period depends on the amplitude.
blocks.solution:
(a) Both systems have Jacobian $\begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ at the origin, a centre, so the linearisation theorem says nothing. Take $V = x^2 + y^2$. For the first system $\dot V = 2x(-y - x^3) + 2y(x - y^3) = -2(x^4 + y^4) < 0$ away from the origin, so by Lyapunov's theorem the origin is asymptotically stable. For the second, $\dot V = 2(x^4 + y^4) > 0$: the distance to the origin always increases, so the origin is unstable. The cubic terms, invisible to the linearisation, decide.

(b) The linearisation at the origin is $\begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, which has a zero eigenvalue and decides nothing. The energy $H = \frac12y^2 + \frac14x^4$ is conserved, and its level sets are closed curves around the origin, so every solution is periodic. Scaling: if $x(t)$ is a solution, then so is $X(t) = Ax(At)$, since $X'' = A^3x''(At) = -A^3x(At)^3 = -X^3$. If $x$ has amplitude 1 and period $T_1$, then $X$ has amplitude $A$ and period $T_1/A$. Larger swings are faster, unlike the linear spring, whose period does not depend on amplitude. For amplitude 1, $H = \frac14$ and $y = \sqrt{(1 - x^4)/2}$ on the way across, so

$$T_1 = 4\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{(1 - x^4)/2}} = 4\sqrt2\int_0^1\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1 - x^4}} \approx 7.416.$$

blocks.body:
- A linear centre in the Jacobian does not mean the nonlinear system has a centre; use a conserved quantity or a Lyapunov function.
- Linearisation is local. A stable node at one equilibrium says nothing about solutions starting far away; basins of attraction are bounded by separatrices such as the stable manifolds of saddles.
- Nullclines are not trajectories: a trajectory crosses the $x$-nullcline vertically and the $y$-nullcline horizontally.
- A Lyapunov function must be positive away from the equilibrium on a whole neighbourhood; a $V$ with $\dot V < 0$ that is not positive definite proves nothing about stability.

When a parameter in the system changes, equilibria can appear, disappear or change stability, which is the subject of [[bifurcations]]. Trajectories that are closed but isolated, unlike the family of orbits around a centre, are limit cycles; in the plane the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem gives a way to prove they exist, see [[limit-cycles]]. In three or more dimensions trajectories have more room, and bounded solutions can wander forever without settling down or repeating, which is [[chaos]]. Numerically, phase portraits are drawn with the methods of [[numerical-odes]], and the gradient flows behind [[gradient-descent]] are systems for which the function being minimised is a Lyapunov function.

1. Classify the origin for $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ with $A = \begin{pmatrix}-2 & 1\\ -5 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and sketch the phase portrait.
2. Find and classify all equilibria of $x' = y$, $y' = x - x^3$, and find a conserved quantity.
3. For the damped pendulum $x' = y$, $y' = -\sin x - cy$ with $c > 0$, find for which $c$ the origin is a stable spiral and for which it is a stable node.
4. Show that $V = x^2 + 2y^2$ proves asymptotic stability of the origin for $x' = -x + 2y^2$, $y' = -xy - y^3$.
